title: Chapter 67 – Spring Register
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Lin Jian]

The Gate Hall holds three hundred children, and not one of them is speaking above a whisper.

Jian stands in the third rank of the queue with his pack on his back and his right hand wrapped in clean linen. The hall is a long, high, drafty place of black pillars and pale stone, with a ceiling lost in shadow and a floor worn into shallow troughs by a hundred years of nervous feet. Banners of cloud-blue silk hang from the rafters. At the far end, on a low dais of white jade, sits a bronze disc as wide as a cart wheel, set on edge in a stand of black wood. The Register Mirror.

He has been looking at it for an hour. It does not look back.

The right hand is a nuisance. It is the first thing the fog did at the ford, minutes before Cheng Yun came running: a single drifting thread of red mist that curled round the cart wheel and touched the back of his hand, and the skin rose in blisters like boiled milk. Wenqing's salve has taken the worst of it. The bandage hides the rest. He had thought of it as an inconvenience.

On the road, last night, he had thought of it as a gift.

A child's right palm, he thinks. Eight and a half centimeters. Five fingers a little spread.

Somewhere on a desk in this mountain there is a sketch of that hand, in a tube of oiled paper. It has been six months. It has certainly been read. He does not know by whom.

Left, he thinks. I will offer the left.

He keeps the Seasons Veil turning, shallow and slow, and lets it show a boy of the seventh layer: not a prodigy, not a fool, a farm child with a little talent and a good teacher. It is a considerable weight. His recovery is a fifth down, and the ache behind his eyes has settled in for the day. He bears it.

Not a spectacle, he thinks. A number that does not stand out.

A clerk in a gray robe goes down the queue with a brush and a ledger, writing names. He reaches Jian. He does not look up.

"Name."

"Lin Jian. Green Pine Hill."

The brush stops.

It is the smallest pause. The clerk's eyes come up, quick and sharp, and travel over the boy's face and the linen on his hand. Then he looks down again, and writes, and the line he writes is a short one.

"Registered by letter," he says. "Stand to the left of the dais, with the others of your sort. There are four."

Four, thinks Jian. Four who were chosen before they came.

He goes where he is told.

* * *

They call the others first.

It takes the whole morning. One by one, the children climb the three steps of the dais, and a registrar in a robe of blue and gray lays a small bronze rod against the Mirror's edge. The disc wakes. Light moves across it, slow, silver, like moonlight on a pond. Each child puts a palm to the glass, and the light shifts and steadies, and shows a number, and the registrar reads it aloud.

Qi Refining, one. A murmur. Two. A sigh. One. Three, and a little ripple of interest. Most of them are one or two. A tall, hard-faced boy of thirteen is called a four, and carries himself down the steps like a man collecting a debt. A girl in green silk is a five, and does not smile at all.

In the gallery that runs along the east wall, behind a low rail of lacquered wood, the Elders sit.

Jian counts them. There are nine. They do not look at the children. They sit with their hands in their sleeves and their faces calm, in robes of deep blue and gray and one of white, and they watch the Mirror as a farmer watches a field. At the end of the row there is a stout, ruddy man with ash-stained cuffs, eating a dried plum. Beside him, a lean scholar with a long gray beard and a quiet, tired face. In the center, in white, with a tally-stick laid across his knees, a man Jian knows.

Shen Wuye.

He has not changed. He is lean and pale and still, with a face like a closed book. The Arbiter has been to the hill, once, in the autumn, and sat in the study, and delivered a ruling that cost Wenyuan a night's sleep and the clan a quarter of its stones. He is not looking at the Mirror. He is looking, with great, unhurried attention, at the left-hand side of the dais, where the four registered by letter stand.

His eyes rest on each of them in turn. They rest on Jian a little longer.

He has the sketch, thinks Jian, coldly. Or has read it.

It is not an accusation. It is a fact, laid on the table like a coin.

The registrar calls his name at noon.

"Lin Jian, of Green Pine Hill. Come forward."

He climbs the steps. He is aware of the hall behind him, the long, hushed, curious breath of three hundred children and their guardians. Against a far pillar, a lean man in a gray cloak has not moved since dawn. He does not look at him.

He stops before the Mirror. It is larger than he thought. He can see himself in it, a small gray figure with a bandaged hand, dwarfed by the polished bronze.

"The right palm," says the registrar. He is a thin, dry man with a bored voice.

"It is burned." Jian holds it up. "Yesterday. From a Blood Shadow fog, on the Cloud Road. May I offer the left?"

There is a pause.

"A Blood Shadow fog?" says someone in the gallery, quite audibly.

The registrar glances along the row of Elders, as if for a ruling. The stout man with the plum has stopped chewing. The scholar has inclined his head. In the center, in white, the Arbiter says nothing.

"The Mirror reads either," says the registrar, at last. "It is the Qi, not the hand." He waves it. "Left."

Not the hand, thinks Jian. Good.

He lays his left palm against the cold bronze.

For a long moment, nothing happens.

Then the Mirror wakes.

It does not do it as it did for the others. The silver light does not drift. It comes up from beneath the glass like something rising through deep water, slow, steady, enormous, and fills the whole disc with a pale cold radiance that throws his shadow across the dais. The bronze hums. A fine thin note, high and clear, rises from the stand, and the registrar takes a step back.

Jian has not dropped the Veil.

He remembers it, then. He had meant to. It was the whole plan, the thing he had decided on the long road, in the dark of the cart. Drop it before the Mirror. Let them see what is there. A hidden thing found is a thing that is hunted. A thing shown is a thing that is only a fact.

He lets it go.

It falls from him like a cloak. The false wheel stops, and the true one, deep and dark and heavy, rolls forward into the light, and the Mirror takes it.

The numbers rise.

They climb the glass in tall gold characters, slowly, one after another, as if the Mirror were reluctant to believe them. Qi Refining. Layer. A stroke. Layer. Another. The registrar has stopped breathing. The characters crawl upward past the seventh, and the eighth, and stop.

Nine.

Not a light nine. A heavy one, deep and ringed, the kind that sits at the bottom of a pool. A faint pale arc, a curve of seasonal light, runs round the number like a halo. And then, as the Mirror seems to remember its manners, a second line of characters: Peak. Qi: ringed, seasonal.

The hall is silent.

It is not the silence of three hundred children who have been told to be quiet. It is the silence of a room in which a very large thing has just been set down on a table.

"Qi Refining," says the registrar. His voice has gone high and thin. "Ninth. Peak." He swallows. "He is..." He does not finish.

He takes his hand from the Mirror. The light dies slowly, and the bronze goes dark.

In the gallery, a cup falls, and breaks.

It is the plum-eater. He is on his feet with the cup in pieces at his sandals and his round face gone pale beneath the flush, staring at the dais with an expression of pure, naked greed. The scholar has not moved at all, but his eyes are very bright. Along the rail, the other Elders have begun, in low voices, to speak. A murmur runs through the hall like wind through grass. Nine. At twenty. The ring. Lin. Which Lin? Green Pine. The hill with the Garden. The boy who...

And in the center of the gallery, in white, the Arbiter rises.

He lays the tally-stick on his seat. He looks, across forty paces, directly at the boy on the dais, and his face does not change at all. After a moment, he inclines his head, a shallow, perfectly correct bow.

It is a courtesy, and Jian does not trust it for a heartbeat.

"Order," says the registrar. He has found his voice. "Order! The disciple will step down. The next..."

He steps down.

His legs, he finds, are not quite steady. He walks down the three steps and across the white floor with his bandaged hand held against his chest, and the children part before him like water. Many of them are staring. A few look afraid. One boy, a big heavy-set lad in a blue tunic, grins at him, wide and delighted, as though he had just seen a dog do a trick.

Cheng Yun is still against his pillar.

He has not moved. His face is as blank as a wall. But as the boy passes, very slowly, he closes one eye.

* * *

The Deacon finds him at the foot of the steps.

He is a soft, round man in a gray robe with a blue collar, perhaps forty-five, with a plump, pleasant face and a small curling mustache and a smile that appears to have been fitted at birth. His thumbs are stained with ink. He is carrying a ledger the size of a doorstop, and two tokens of pale gray jade on a cord.

"Disciple Lin." The smile widens. "A very great honor. A very great honor indeed. I am Deacon Mo Lian, of the Outer Affairs Hall. I have the pleasure of seeing to the registered."

A Deacon's smile is a price, Jian thinks. Ask what it costs.

"Deacon," he says, and bows. It is the correct depth, to the inch. He has practiced.

"Come, come. You are a little pale. It is the long road, I expect." Mo Lian takes his elbow, lightly, and steers him through the crowd with a practiced, gentle pressure, as one steers a mule through a market. "We shall have you seen to at once. It is a rare thing, Lin Jian, to find a talent like yours at the Register. It would be a very great pity if it were wasted on the usual formalities."

"I would be glad of the usual formalities."

"Ha. Of course. Modest, too." The Deacon pats his arm. "Here. Your token."

It is a small slab of gray jade, the size of a thumb, with a hole through the top and a cloud carved on one face. On the other, in neat black characters, is a name and a number. Lin Jian. Outer Sect. 0417.

"The token is your self," says Mo Lian. "It opens your courtyard. It admits you to the grounds. It is entered in the Contribution Register, where your name will remain for as long as you are of the Sect. Do not lose it." He lowers his voice, confidentially. "The fine for a lost token is ten points. A great deal, for a first-year."

"Points?"

"Contribution points. They are earned by service to the Sect, and spent on what the Sect provides. Pills, scriptures, stones, the use of a cultivation chamber. A disciple's rank is his name, but his points are his bread." The smile does not change. "You will learn. It is not complicated. A sensible boy does not need a great deal of explaining."

He is steered to a long wooden counter, where a clerk hands over a short robe of Outer Sect gray with a cloud-blue hem, a plain tunic and leggings, a flat cloth pouch, a wooden bowl and a wooden spoon.

"The monthly allowance is three low stones and one Breath-Gathering Pill," says Mo Lian. "A disciple of your rank is entitled to a place in the Outer courtyards. There is, I fear, some difficulty."

"Difficulty."

"There are three hundred new registrations, and the courtyards fill by rank and by reservation. A boy who is a nine, and a Seal, at twenty..." The Deacon sighs, sorrowfully, like a man describing a fine horse in an inconvenient stable. "He would naturally wish to be placed near the Hundred Veins pool, in the Eastern Court, with the others of his talent. I have written the request. It is, I regret, not quite within my authority."

"I see."

"The usual placement for a first-year, I am sorry to say, is the Reed Courtyard." He turns a page. "At the foot of the mountain. Near the Medicine Valley terraces. A little damp. A little far from the springs. There are seven others in it, all of the first year, all of a more... modest cultivation. I should not like to see a boy like you left to rot in it." A pause, delicately timed. "If, of course, some arrangement could be made."

There it is.

It is, Jian thinks, rather good. It is not an offer. It is the shape of an offer, drawn with such care that it leaves a hollow exactly the size of a bribe. He lets it hang. He looks at the Deacon's face, and at the ink on his thumbs, and at the smile.

The ink is not black.

It is a dark, deep, rusty brown, the color of old blood. It has dried into the creases of the skin on the right thumb, and under the nail. A scholar's stain, it might be. A Deacon's, who writes all day. It might be nothing at all.

He files it.

"I am grateful for the Deacon's concern," he says. "I would prefer to see the Reed Courtyard first."

Something moves behind the smile. It is very small, and very fast: a flicker of calculation, quickly smoothed. Then the Deacon laughs, delighted.

"Quite right! Quite right. A boy who looks before he buys." He writes. "Reed Courtyard, number six. Your bed will be the third from the door. I shall send a servant with your bedding." He lowers his voice again. "We shall speak further, Disciple Lin. In a few days. When you have seen how things stand."

He bustles away into the crowd, with his ledger under his arm, still smiling.

Jian watches him go.

A price, he thinks. Not yet named.

* * *

The Beast Hall is a long, low building at the edge of the Court, built of dark stone and smelling strongly of wet fur.

He goes there alone in the afternoon, with a slip of paper in his hand and the beast bag tied to his belt. A keeper meets him at the door. She is an old woman with a face like a walnut and a scar across one cheek, and she looks at the bag, and at the boy, and at the slip, in that order.

"Hatchling?"

"Yes."

"First rank?"

"I think so."

"You think." She sniffs. "Species?"

"I do not know." It is the one true thing he has said all day. "I found her. In a gully, near my home. She was injured."

"Mm." She does not seem to doubt it. She holds out her hand, and he unties the pouch and gives it to her, and she turns it over with the practiced ease of a woman who has handled ten thousand of them. "Awake?"

He hesitates.

"She sleeps," he says. "A great deal."

"Good. They are easier asleep." The keeper walks him through a narrow door and into a room with a stone table, a brass lamp, and a long slab of dark glass set into the wall. "The Hall scans every creature of every disciple. It is required. A hatchling is no danger, but a thing that grows is a thing that must be known. Put her on the table."

Pebble.

He opens the bag.

She is curled inside it, on a little nest of damp moss, with her nose tucked under her tail and her scales dull and gray in the lamplight. She does not wake. She has not, he realizes, been fully awake since the ford. The bag has a way of doing that. It takes whatever lives in it and pulls it down, gently, into a long still sleep, the way a lake takes a stone.

Pebble?

Nothing.

It is a small, flat silence. It is not unkind. But it is a silence where, for six months, there has been a voice, a quiet, dry, tiny, ever-present voice at the back of his thoughts, and he finds that he did not know how loud it was until it stopped.

He lays her on the stone.

The keeper passes a flat bronze plate above her. The slab of glass in the wall flickers and fills with a pale shape, a small round thing curled in a ball, ringed by a faint thin circle of light. A line of characters scrolls beside it.

Beast. Hatchling. Pangolin, scale-armored. Rank: Level 1, low. Condition: dormant. Notes: injured, healed; bond, voluntary.

Voluntary. He stares at it.

"It reads a bond," says the keeper. "It always does. A hatchling that is bonded of its own will is not a danger, and not property. She may not be taken from you, unless you let her go." She takes the plate away. "Twenty days."

"I beg your pardon?"

"Twenty days asleep. That is how long it takes a hatchling to settle in a bag of that kind, when it is as small as this one. She will not wake before then, and you must not open it more than twice. A long sleep, and a long rest. It is good for the scales." She wraps the creature in a fold of moss and hands her back. "Come and see me on the twenty-first day, if she has not stirred. And boy."

"Yes?"

"Do not feed her on anything but what I tell you." Her scarred face is unreadable. "That is a seamwalker, if I am any judge. A very young one. I have not seen one in thirty years." She turns away. "I did not say so."

He stands in the cold stone room with the small warm weight of the sleeping creature in his hands, and the keeper's words going round in his head like a coin in a cup.

She knew, he thinks. And she has chosen to say nothing.

Why?

It is a question he cannot answer. He puts the bag back at his belt, under the cloak, and goes out into the long gold light of the afternoon. He feels the lack of her at every step, like a stone missing from a wall.

* * *

Feng is waiting at the end of the long gray bridge.

Jian sees him from a hundred paces. He is standing at the rail, with a hand on the stone and his weight on his right leg, tall, thin, with the long, bony shoulders of a man who has trained harder than he has eaten. He wears the Outer Sect gray. He has a scar on his chin that Jian does not recognize. He is looking not at the bridge but at the river beneath it, and he does not move at all, until the boy is twenty paces off.

Then he turns round.

It is a very small moment. Neither of them says a word. Feng's face does something complicated, a spasm of pleasure and dismay and relief, and then settles into a tight, careful calm.

"You are late," he says.

"The road was long."

"The Mirror was noon. It is nearly the third bell." His voice has deepened. It has a rasp in it. "I heard. The whole of the Outer Court heard. A nine, at twenty." A short, hard breath. "You were supposed to be a seven."

"I know."

"I told you to say it was a pill."

"It is not a pill."

"No," says Feng, "I gathered that." He crosses the last twenty paces, and the limp is plain now, a hitch in the left leg, a drag of the foot on the stone. He does not seem to notice it. He stops in front of Jian, and stands there, looking at him, and then, very abruptly, puts out his arms and catches him in a short, hard, awkward hug, and lets go.

"You have grown," he says.

"An inch."

"It is not enough." He steps back and scrubs the heel of his hand across his eyes. "I am not crying. It is the wind."

"There is no wind."

"It is a very small one."

They walk along the bridge together, slowly, because of the leg. The river runs far below, green and cold and loud with spring melt, and the evening is coming on. The Sect rises round them in terrace after terrace, courtyards stacked on courtyards, red roofs and white walls and the dark green of old pines, and above it all, the long staircase of lights climbing into the dusk. Jian looks at it. He does not say anything.

"I have been counting them," says Feng, quietly. "Every night. Forty, to the lock. I have not told anyone."

"I know."

"It is lit, you know. Tonight. They light it for the Register. The whole stair." He is looking up. "But the last forty are the only ones that have never gone out. In all the months I have been here, in storm, in dark of the moon. They burn white. I asked a Keeper why. He said it was an old array. I asked him what it guarded. He said, nothing you need to know."

"Have you been to it?"

"Every night."

"Have you touched it?"

"Not once." Feng's voice is very low. "It is not the kind of thing you touch, Jian. It is the kind of thing that looks at you. I have stood in front of it, in the dark, for an hour at a time, and I have felt it decide whether I was worth the trouble."

And decide, thinks Jian, and not trouble.

He looks at his brother. At the hard, tired, twenty-six-year-old face, and the hands, which have a new set of calluses, and the left leg, which drags.

"How is the leg?" he says.

"It flares." Feng does not look at him. "When I push. When I try the second rank. It is the scar. It is as if the whole thing wakes up, down in the bone, and starts to count. I have tried three times. I have not yet reached the end of the fourth breath." A short, humorless laugh. "I am a first-ranker, and a failure. It is quite a feat."

"It is not a failure. It is a block."

"What is the difference?"

"A block has a cause," says Jian. "We will find it."

It is a promise. It is the second he has made today, and the first he has made aloud. Feng looks at him sidelong, for a moment, with an expression that is not quite hope, and not quite the lack of it.

"There is someone you should see," he says.

He does not point. He only tilts his head, a little, toward the far end of the bridge, where a stone lantern stands beside the steps. A boy is leaning against it with his arms folded. He is fourteen, tall and fair and sharp-featured, in a gray robe cut a good deal finer than any Jian has seen in the Court. A silver pin holds back his hair. He has the clear, cold, perfect face of a person who has never been told no.

He is looking at Jian. He has been, Jian realizes, for some time.

"Zhao Yao," says Feng, very quietly. "Red Ridge. Heng's cousin. He came last year. He has said nothing to me, in all that time, that was not a sneer. But he has been watching you since you came onto the bridge." A pause. "He has been watching the hill. Since the siege. He asks about it. Every week."

Jian does not look away.

For a long moment, the two of them regard each other across forty paces of evening air. Then Zhao Yao unfolds his arms, slowly, and straightens off the lantern, and lifts one hand in a gesture that is almost a salute. It is not friendly. It is not hostile. It is a gesture that means: I know what you are, and I will wait.

Then he turns, and walks off, and the shadow of the great stair swallows him.

* * *

The Reed Courtyard is at the very bottom of the mountain, where the paving gives up and the wet begins.

It is a square of beaten earth, thirty paces on a side, ringed by a low wall of mossy stone and a row of reeds, and floored with the last of the snowmelt. Four small buildings stand round it, each of two rooms, each with a sagging tile roof and a door that does not quite close. The air is thick and damp and faintly sour. It smells of mud and of old rain. When he draws a breath, it is thin as watered wine: a half of what the Green Pine Hill gave him, and a third of what the upper courts must have.

The qi is poor here, he thinks. It is meant to be.

He is the last of the eight. They are in the central room, on straw pallets, laughing and quarreling over the single lamp: a big fair boy called Ma Bao, who grins at him without reserve; a small silent one who does not look up; a sharp-faced youth of thirteen with a stolen apple. They fall silent when he comes in, and stare at him, and then, one by one, begin to speak all at once.

He answers them politely. He says as little as he can. He learns that there is a spring at the end of the lane for water, and a latrine behind the wall, and a bell at dawn for chores, and that the Deacon has made it plain that any disciple who is late shall be fined a point. He says that he is tired. He is given a bed.

It is the third from the door, as promised. A narrow wooden frame with a straw tick and a gray blanket, under a window that looks out onto the reeds.

He sits down on it, with his hands between his knees, and listens to the clatter of spoons in the other room. He thinks of a hammer ringing in a cold forge, and a lamp his mother will have left lit. He thinks of a small weight in the bag at his belt, and the silence where a voice should be.

Twenty days, he thinks.

He lies back, at last, with the token on its cord round his neck, and stares at the underside of the roof. It is stained and mottled, with a long brown water mark like a map of a country that does not exist.

He turns his head.

The cot's wooden frame is a simple thing, four posts and two rails, rough-planed and unvarnished. The rail nearest his face has a crack running along it, an old split, and beneath the crack, on the inner side, where no one would look who was not lying exactly where he lies, someone has scratched a mark.

It is very small. It is not carved; it is scored, with the point of a knife, in a few quick strokes. A little knot of three lines, pulled tight at the center, with a single short thread trailing from the last.

It is not new, and not old. The wood in the scratches is pale.

He does not move.

Blood Shadow, he thinks. A thread-knot.

He has seen it before. He has seen it on a wall at the Garden, on a map in Hu's forge, on the cloth of a dead man's cuff. It is a sign. A mark of the kind they leave when a place has been chosen, or looked at, or promised to someone.

He thinks of a round man's smile, and the rust-brown ink under his thumbnail, and a bed that was chosen for him before he arrived.

He lies in the dark, very quietly, under the sagging roof, and listens to the reeds.
